name: Zolpidem (Ambien)

card.summary: A prescription Z-drug sleeping pill with a boxed warning for complex sleep behaviors; no appearance research exists.
card.aka: Ambien, Ambien CR, Stilnox, Edluar, Intermezzo
card.note: Controlled substance (US Schedule IV); FDA boxed warning for sleepwalking-type behaviors; tolerance and dependence reported.

quick.overview:
Zolpidem is a nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic sold as Ambien, first used in Europe in 1988 and approved in the US in 1992. It is prescribed for short-term insomnia.

It appears in looksmaxxing recovery discussion as one prescription route to sleep. No study has tested it for any appearance outcome, and its published research concerns insomnia, memory and brain activity.
quick.mechanism: Zolpidem is a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors, binding at the benzodiazepine site. Its half-life in healthy adults is about 2 to 3 hours.
quick.risks: Reported effects include next-day impairment, memory problems, hallucinations, falls and impaired driving. In 2019 the FDA added a boxed warning about complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-driving. Tolerance and dependence are reported, and it is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.

lead: Zolpidem is a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic, or Z-drug, sold under brand names including Ambien. It was first used in Europe in 1988 by Synthelabo, approved in the US in 1992, and became available as a generic in 2007 [1]. It is indicated for short-term treatment of insomnia, typically two to six weeks [1].
In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned as a prescription option within sleep optimisation. No published study has examined zolpidem for appearance outcomes.

A 2005 review described it as improving sleep with favourable tolerability when used as labelled [2], while later regulatory actions, including lowered recommended doses in 2013 and a boxed warning in 2019, addressed next-morning impairment and complex sleep behaviors [1].
infobox: About 2 to 3 hours in healthy adults [1]
Ambien, Ambien CR, Edluar, Intermezzo, ZolpiMist
US Schedule IV; controlled in Canada and UK; prescription-only in Australia [1]

paras: Zolpidem is used for short-term insomnia at the lowest effective dose. Guidelines from NICE, the European Sleep Research Society and the American College of Physicians recommend it only after non-drug approaches such as cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia [1]. Off-label uses such as disorders of consciousness and post-stroke aphasia have been explored, with unclear benefit [1].

Wikipedia summarises that it shortens time to fall asleep by about 15 minutes, with higher doses helping people stay asleep longer, and notes a 2012 review concluding that much of the effect is psychological [1]. A 2005 review described it as improving sleep with a low propensity for residual effects, withdrawal or dependence when used according to prescribing information [2].

Common effects include daytime sleepiness, headache, dizziness, nausea and diarrhea. Serious effects reported include memory problems, hallucinations, depression, falls, fractures and impaired driving [1]. A case report literature has linked hallucinations to combined use with serotonin reuptake inhibitors [3].
Complex sleep behaviors such as walking, driving or eating while asleep, with amnesia, led the FDA to add a boxed warning in April 2019 and a contraindication for people with a previous episode [1].

Tolerance can develop within weeks, and abrupt withdrawal after prolonged use can cause seizures or delirium, so gradual tapering is typical [1]. A study of zolpidem in pregnancy examined placental passage and outcomes [4].

Zolpidem enhances GABA-A receptor signalling at the benzodiazepine site, with structural determinants of its high-affinity binding characterised in laboratory work [5]. Research has also examined its effects on sleep spindles and on synchrony of brain activity [6][7].
Oral bioavailability is about 70 percent and protein binding about 92 percent. It is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4, with CYP2C9 and CYP1A2 contributing, into metabolites considered inactive [1].

No studies have examined zolpidem for appearance outcomes. Research on it concerns insomnia and cognition. A pharmacology study found that zolpidem increased sleep spindles during a nap and was associated with improved memory consolidation [6], and a related study reported enhanced recognition of negative and high-arousal memories [7]. A 2013 comparison reported that orexin receptor antagonists promoted sleep at doses that did not disrupt cognition in the way zolpidem and eszopiclone did [8].

Registered trials include a 67-person phase 4 comparison of sublingual and oral formulations in primary insomnia [9] and a 132-person phase 4 comparison of modified-release and standard zolpidem [10].
Zolpidem is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US and in Canada, and Class C in the UK [1]. Brand names include Ambien, Ambien CR, Edluar, Intermezzo and ZolpiMist [1].
